clinicalPearls: Autosomal dominant disorder caused by variants in ATP2A2, which encodes the SERCA2 endoplasmic reticulum calcium pump
Presents in adolescence with greasy, warty, malodorous keratotic papules coalescing in seborrhoeic distribution (chest, back, scalp margins, flexures)
Nail changes are highly characteristic: alternating red and white longitudinal bands with distal V-shaped nicks
Palmar pits and punctate keratoses, plus mucosal cobblestone papules, support the diagnosis
Heat, sweating, sunlight, and friction typically exacerbate the eruption, so flares are common in summer
Neuropsychiatric associations, including mood disorders, are recognised in affected families
Superimposed herpes simplex (Kaposi varicelliform eruption) can cause abrupt, painful deterioration
reference.pathophysiology: Darier disease results from loss-of-function variants in ATP2A2, encoding the SERCA2 pump that transports calcium into the endoplasmic reticulum of keratinocytes. Impaired intracellular calcium regulation disrupts the calcium-dependent assembly and function of desmosomal adhesion complexes. The consequence is loss of cohesion between keratinocytes (acantholysis) together with abnormal keratinisation of individual cells (dyskeratosis), giving the histological hallmarks of suprabasal acantholysis with corps ronds and grains. Environmental triggers such as heat, ultraviolet light, and mechanical friction further destabilise the fragile epidermis and precipitate clinical flares.
additionalDifferentials: Pemphigus (vegetans/foliaceus) in flexural or eroded forms
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy showing suprabasal acantholysis with dyskeratotic corps ronds and grains
Viral swab or PCR for herpes simplex when sudden painful worsening occurs
Bacterial swabs of malodorous or eroded lesions
Family history and examination of nails and mucosa for corroborating signs
redFlags: Sudden painful monomorphic vesicles or erosions suggesting Kaposi varicelliform eruption from herpes superinfection
Widespread erosions with systemic upset and secondary bacterial infection
Rapidly enlarging or ulcerated lesion raising concern for squamous change
reference.prognosis: It is a chronic, relapsing condition that persists lifelong with seasonal flares, but most patients maintain reasonable control with skin care, avoidance of triggers, and oral retinoids in severe cases; it does not shorten life expectancy.
pitfalls: Missing herpes superinfection and attributing a painful flare simply to disease activity
Mistaking flexural involvement for intertrigo or fungal infection
Overlooking the characteristic nail and palmar signs that clinch the diagnosis
Failing to advise on heat, sweat, and sun avoidance that reduces flares
management: Advise avoidance of triggers such as heat, sweating, sunlight and friction, with cool loose clothing, sun protection and regular emollients
Treat mild to moderate disease with topical retinoids, topical corticosteroids and keratolytics
Use oral retinoids such as acitretin for severe or widespread disease
Treat secondary bacterial infection with antibiotics, and superimposed herpes simplex (Kaposi varicelliform eruption) promptly with antiviral therapy
Manage malodour and maceration in flexures with antiseptics and topical antimicrobials
Screen for and support associated neuropsychiatric conditions such as mood disorders
Offer genetic counselling for this autosomal dominant ATP2A2 disorder, and consider dermatological surgery or laser for resistant localised disease
